issues: Whether settlement payments, interest, and legal fees paid to resolve a securities class action and bankruptcy estate claims are deductible as business expenses under s. 9 of the Income Tax Act.

Whether the 'egregious or repulsive' conduct exception can bar a deduction where no court has found the taxpayer committed any wrongdoing and the settlement was paid without an admission of liability.

Whether the Crown's reply, containing extensive assumptions of fact characterizing the taxpayer's conduct as fraud and aiding fraud, complies with the rules of pleading in the Tax Court and should be struck or ordered amended.
Whether the Crown may plead fraud as an assumption of fact in a reply, thereby shifting the burden of proof to the taxpayer to disprove fraud it was never found to have committed.
Whether the Crown may rely on the conduct of third parties to deny a deduction to the taxpayer.
Whether the Crown's recharacterization of structured financings as 'disguised loans' is a proper issue in a tax appeal and is adequately pleaded.
The procedural test and standard for striking or amending a pleading in the Tax Court, including whether a pleading that is scandalous, frivolous, or an abuse of process may be struck.
Whether the inclusion of third-party material, foreign pleadings, and identification of dismissed employees in the Crown's reply is relevant and proper.
key_facts: Client is a large Canadian financial institution that participated in structured financing deals with a major energy company through foreign affiliates.
The energy company collapsed amid an accounting scandal.
Client was named in a securities class action and in claims brought by the energy company's bankruptcy estate.
Client settled both suits for several billion dollars with no court ruling on whether it had done anything wrong.
Client deducted the settlement payments, interest, and legal fees as business expenses.
On appeal, the Crown filed a reply of over 80 pages, roughly 70 of which are assumptions of fact.
The Crown repeatedly characterizes the financings as 'disguised loans.'
The Crown asserts the client knowingly aided fraud and falsified financial statements.
The Crown recites at length the conduct and internal affairs of the energy company and other third parties.
The Crown quotes from U.S. pleadings and names employees who were dismissed.
The Crown's theory is that conduct so 'egregious or repulsive' bars deduction regardless of income-earning purpose.
The Crown pleads all of this as assumptions of fact, which would put the burden on the client to disprove fraud it was never found to have committed.
causes_of_action: Motion to strike the Crown's reply in its entirety or in part
Motion to order the Crown to amend its reply to remove fraud characterizations, third-party material, and evidentiary material
Objection to the Crown's 'egregious or repulsive' theory as a matter of law
candidate_statutes: Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), s. 9
Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)), s. 67
search_terms: settlement payment without admission of liability deduction
